title: Task Memory Engine (TME): Enhancing State Awareness for Multi-Step LLM Agent Tasks
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 14, 15, 16 of 16; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: The Task Memory Tree (TMT) is an externalised structure the agent writes to at run time: 'nodes are dynamically created and updated in real time' as the agent progresses through a task (Sec. 4.1, p. 4). The Prompt Synthesizer then reads that structure back — 'traverses the active node path — from the root to the current leaf — and generates a concise, contextually-relevant prompt' (p. 4) — conditioning the agent's subsequent behaviour. This is a run-time write/read loop over agent-authored state, not a fixed corpus or parametric-only mechanism, satisfying I1. The record is 2025 (p. 1), in English, and is 16 pages with full text available, so I2-I4 hold and no exclusion criterion applies: memory is the paper's entire contribution (contributions 1-4, p. 2), not incidental (rules out E5), and the store is written by the agent, not a fixed index (rules out E3).

facets.justification: The Task Memory Tree is a hierarchical node/edge structure the agent writes: each node holds action, input/output, status, and explicit 'Parent/Children' and 'Dependencies' cross-links (Sec. 4.1, p. 4). The paper explicitly frames it as graph-structured: 'TMT is already approaching a relaxed DAG form, which lays the foundation for future graph-based memory extensions' (p. 5).

Nodes are not merely appended: they are 'dynamically created and updated in real time' (p. 4), and TRIM performs 'subtree pruning and merging' to reduce redundancy (p. 4) plus rollback/replacement/merge operations that revert or overwrite existing nodes as new instructions arrive (Sec. 4.2.2, p. 5; Sec. 4.2.7, p. 6: 'Merged Task = f(Task1, Task2)', pruning via arg min cost).

Re-entry into context is a deterministic tree traversal, not a ranked or agent-issued lookup: 'A dedicated Prompt Synthesizer traverses the active node path — from the root to the current leaf — and generates a concise, contextually-relevant prompt' (Sec. 4.1, p. 4).

The abstract states the method is demonstrated 'through case studies and comparative experiments on multi-step agent tasks' (p. 1) against a baseline (full-history prompting), not deployed with real users or in a fielded setting (p. 14-15). No deployment, production use, or external stakeholder is reported in the given pages, so this is a lab-investigated technique, coded conservatively as validation rather than evaluation.

The evidence given is a worked example, not a benchmark suite: Table 3 (p. 15) walks a specific form-filling interaction across six rounds comparing the Baseline and TET (structured-memory) prompt construction, and p. 5 lists the scenario types studied ('recipe adaptation, travel itinerary revisions, or multi-tab planning'). p. 14 references a token-efficiency comparison ('Table 1') but that table's contents were not among the extracted pages, so it cannot independently be verified as a benchmark suite.

Contribution 1 (p. 2) names the deliverable as 'a novel memory framework composed of the Task Memory Tree (TMT) and the Task Planner' — an architecture of three interacting components (TMT, TRIM, Prompt Synthesizer, p. 1) rather than a single technique. Code is released (contribution 6, p. 2) but is presented as an implementation of the framework, not the contribution itself.

title: Memory as a Controlled Process: Learned Adaptive Memory Management for LLM Agents
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 4, 7, 15, 30, 31, 32 of 32; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: The contribution is a controller (MemCon) that decides, task by task, when to write to and read from an agent's own experience store: it wraps the retrieve/store entry points of a memory backend and issues RETRIEVE, PLAN_INJECT, RE-RETRIEVE, CONSOLIDATE, and FORGET actions whose effects condition the agent's behaviour on later tasks (p. 2, p. 4 Fig. 1). The policy itself 'persists to disk between tasks' and is 'updated via reverse-discounted credit assignment from binary task success' (p. 2), i.e. state written at run time is read back across sessions to shape future action selection. Preprint dated 2026 on the title page (I2); written in English (I3); full text was retrievable, evidenced by the extracted pages (I4). Not excluded: memory here is not incidental (it is the entire subject of the abstract and contributions, p. 1-2), the paper is a primary empirical study, not a survey (E4 does not hold), and the system is explicitly an LLM agent framework evaluated across three agent runners and three LLM backbones (p. 2, p. 7), so E6 does not hold. The paper explicitly disclaims being 'a new memory store' (p. 2), which raised the E1/E3 question, but the guide's own boundary resolves it: deciding what is retrieved, injected, consolidated, or forgotten is a policy over what persists, not an architecture-only change, and the backend it controls (e.g. G-Memory in the reported results, p. 7, p. 15) is itself written to at run time rather than a fixed corpus.

facets.justification: The paper states directly: 'MemCon is not a new memory store. It is a thin wrapper that intercepts the abstract retrieve and store entry points of any existing memory backend and decides how to call them... The same wrapper applies unchanged to flat vector stores, skill libraries, summarisation-based memories, latent-token memories, and graph-structured memories' (p. 2). The contribution therefore has no single owned substrate among the listed categories; it is substrate-agnostic by design. For the reported main results the wrapper is plugged into one fixed backend, G-Memory, described as combining vector retrieval, a task graph with k-hop traversal, and insight rules (p. 15, A.3 item 9; also used in the Section 4 evaluation, p. 7), which is recorded under secondary_substrates rather than coded as primary since it is a pre-existing baseline system MemCon controls, not what MemCon itself contributes.

The action space explicitly includes CONSOLIDATE and FORGET as discrete controller-selected actions: 'C ONSOLIDATE and F ORGET call any maintenance hooks the backend exposes (e.g., merging or pruning derived rules) and silently no-op on backends that do not implement them' (p. 4). The contribution is precisely the decision of when to trigger a write/maintenance action; the paper leaves the actual transformation (merge vs. prune logic) to whichever backend is plugged in and does not specify it generally, matching the guide's reservation of agent_tool_invoked for cases where agent control over the write is the contribution and the transformation itself is unspecified.

The controller 'adaptively decides when, what, and how much to retrieve, when to inject a distilled plan, and when to consolidate or forget' (p. 2), selecting a memory action a = (op, θ) including RETRIEVE (with top_k/hop parameters), RE-RETRIEVE (an alternative-query reformulation), and PLAN_INJECT via a UCB policy over a learned Q-table (p. 4, Actions A). This is the agent's own controller choosing what to look for and when, rather than a fixed similarity or recency rule applied uniformly.

Evaluated on 6 public benchmarks (ALFWorld, PDDL Planning, ScienceWorld, TriviaQA, WebWalkerQA, GAIA) against 9 re-implemented memory baselines and a no-memory ablation, across 3 agent frameworks and 3 LLM backbones (p. 2, p. 7 Sec. 4.1). No real users, fielded deployment, or external stakes are reported; results are reported as 'a single deployment run per configuration, no seed averaging' (p. 7) meaning one execution pass per benchmark configuration, not a real-world deployment. This is a controlled, lab-run comparison, so validation rather than evaluation.

Section 4.2 reports 'Table 1 reports S/A on the GPT-4.1-mini backbone' with per-backbone tables for the other two backbones, comparing MemCon against nine baselines over the fixed six-benchmark suite (p. 7) - a fixed task suite with scores reported per system, the defining pattern of benchmark_evaluation.

Contributions list item 2 (p. 2): 'We propose an online contextual bandit policy with UCB exploration, warm-start priors, and reverse-discounted credit assignment that converges within tens of tasks using zero pretraining and zero extra LLM calls, together with augmented memory operations.' This is an algorithmic technique (the MDP formulation plus the bandit learning rule); code is released (p. 1 GitHub link) but the paper argues for the algorithm itself, not the released artefact as the contribution.

title: Adaptive Memory Admission Control for LLM Agents
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 11, 12 of 12; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: Section 3.1 (p. 3) defines memory admission as a run-time decision problem: given conversation history H and an existing memory store M, the agent extracts candidate memories from the dialogue and decides at run time to admit, merge, or reject each one, updating M for use in later turns; Algorithm 1 (p. 5) implements this write/update loop and Section 4 evaluates it on the multi-session LoCoMo benchmark. This is a run-time write to an externalised store that conditions future behaviour, not a fixed corpus or parametric-only mechanism, so none of E1-E7 apply.

facets.justification: Section 3.2 (p. 5), Eq. 3: novelty N(m) is computed by embedding candidates and existing memories with Sentence-BERT and taking max cosine similarity against the store, with embeddings for existing memories precomputed — the memory store is represented and compared as embeddings. The extracted pages do not describe any other storage schema (no SQL, graph, or file structure mentioned), so this is the best-supported reading.

Algorithm 1 (p. 5), lines 5-10: when a candidate conflicts with an existing memory (semantic similarity above 0.85) and scores higher, the framework replaces the existing entry with Merge(m, mconflict); Section 3.3 (p. 5) states this is done explicitly 'to ensure that long-term memory remains compact and up to date.' The no-conflict branch simply appends, but the merge/overwrite behaviour is the mechanism the paper designs and describes as central to admission control, so edit_in_place is coded over plain append_only.

The extracted pages (1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10-12) describe only the admission side — how candidates are scored and written into M — and the evaluation in Section 4 measures admission precision/recall/F1 (Table 1) and feature ablations (Table 2), not how admitted memories are later queried or re-enter context for downstream tasks. No retrieval mechanism for future turns is stated in the given pages, so this is not decidable from what was extracted.

Section 4.1 (p. 6): evaluated on the LoCoMo benchmark (30 conversations, ~1,500 candidate memories) with a train/validation/test split and four baselines (Random, MemGPT, MemoryBank, A-mem); Section 4.3 reports an ablation study (p. 6). This is a controlled benchmark comparison with no reported deployment or real users, i.e. a novel technique investigated in the lab.

Table 1 (p. 6) reports precision/recall/F1/latency for A-MAC against four baselines on the fixed LoCoMo test set (N=225); Table 2 (p. 6) reports ablation results on the same benchmark. Fixed task suite with reported scores across systems.

The contribution list (p. 2, item 2) names the admission scoring technique itself — five interpretable signals combined via learned weights and a threshold rule (Algorithm 1, p. 5). Code is released (p. 1 abstract, GitHub link) but the paper's argument centers on the decision rule/algorithm rather than the artefact.

title: WebATLAS: An LLM Agent with Experience-Driven Memory and Action Simulation
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 10, 11, 12 of 12; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: WebATLAS runs a curiosity-driven exploration pass to seed a cognitive map from interaction experience, then reads that map online during task execution to simulate action outcomes and pick the next action, and also writes to it online 'when execution encounters unseen transitions or world dynamics' (p. 6, Sec 3.3). This is agent-authored, run-time state that conditions the agent's own future behaviour across steps and (via the pre-seeded map) across the whole subsequent episode, satisfying I1. The paper is a 2025 arXiv/NeurIPS-workshop paper in English (p. 1) with full text retrievable (I2-I4). No exclusion applies: the store is agent-written (not E3), memory is one of the three contributions named on p. 2 and in the title (not E5), it is a primary study proposing WebATLAS, not a survey (not E4), and the paper spans at least 11 pages of body/references (not E7).

facets.justification: Sec 3.3, p. 5: the cognitive map is 'represented by tuples (ot, at, ot+1)' and described as 'A graph of transitions M = {(o, a, o′)}' (p. 4, Sec 3.2). This is the store the paper formalizes, builds via a dedicated section (3.3), and repeatedly queries for look-ahead simulation (Sec 3.4, p. 6). Secondary stores: Working Memory ('facts and observations are optionally stored into the LLM context', p. 4 -> prompt_resident) and Semantic Memory / world knowledge (p. 4, 6), whose storage format is not specified in the given pages, coded 'other'.

p. 5-6, Sec 3.3: 'we employ an LLM to convert the trajectories to agentic summaries of the environmental transitions' and the memory agent 'produces concise summaries emphasizing... Differences between successive observations... Newly available actions', explicitly done to avoid 'HTML bloat' (p. 2). Raw transitions are condensed into compact natural-language deltas on write, rather than stored verbatim or synthesized into novel higher-level lessons.

p. 6, Sec 3.3: 'the cognitive map is queried with (ot, at), returning the next raw observation ot+1, as well as LLM summaries.' This is an exact key lookup/graph traversal on the (state, action) pair, not a similarity ranking; Eq. 4 (p. 6) shows this lookup invoked for every action candidate at every step, not an agent-chosen optional read.

Evidence is a benchmark comparison: 'We evaluate WebATLAS on the WebArena-Lite benchmark for autonomous web navigation and demonstrate a success rate of 63%, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art at 53.9%' (p. 1, Abstract), plus ablation studies (p. 1). No deployment, real users, or fielded setting is reported in the given pages, so this is a novel technique investigated in the lab, not evaluation-in-practice.

p. 1, Abstract: success rate reported on the WebArena-Lite benchmark against a prior state-of-the-art figure (63% vs 53.9%), i.e., running the system over a fixed task suite and reporting scores; ablation studies are mentioned as complementary evidence but the headline result is benchmark scoring.

p. 2 contribution list: 'A practical modular architecture that integrates planning, memory, and simulation to transform high-level instructions into safe, executable action sequences', and Sec 3.2 (p. 4) describes WebATLAS as 'four modules operating in an inference-time actor-critic loop' — the paper argues for the overall modular system architecture (planner, actor, critic, multi-layer memory), not a single algorithm or a released tool/dataset.

title: RecMem: Recurrence-based Memory Consolidation for Efficient and Effective Long-Running LLM Agents
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 4, 12, 13, 23, 24, 25 of 25; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: The agent writes run-time state and reads it back to condition later behaviour: interactions are appended to a subconscious vector store, and when a recurrence threshold is met the system promotes them into episodic and semantic memory that is later retrieved to answer questions (pp. 2, 4). Year 2026 satisfies I2 (arXiv timestamp 15 May 2026, p. 1), text is English (I3), and full text was retrievable (I4). No exclusion applies: this is not a hardware/cache paper (E1 n/a), an externalised store is written and read, not parametric-only (E2 n/a), the store is agent-written rather than fixed (E3 n/a), it is a novel-method paper, not a survey (E4 n/a), memory consolidation is the paper's entire contribution (E5 n/a), the system is explicitly an LLM-based agent (E6 n/a), and the paper is a full 25-page article, not abstract-only (E7 n/a).

facets.justification: Section 3.2 (p. 4): the subconscious memory store S_sub is 'implemented as a vector database to support efficient semantic retrieval'; the episodic store is likewise queried by embedding similarity ('retrieve the nearest neighbor episode E* ... v_E* = Φ(E*)', p. 4). All memory tiers described in the extracted pages are embedding/similarity-based, so this is coded as a single vector_store rather than multi_store — no other physical substrate type (graph, relational, filesystem, kv-cache) is used for RecMem's own memory.

On recurrence, 'LLMs are utilized to extract episodic summaries and semantic facts from these interactions' (p. 2); episodic memory 'captures event-level structure across multiple turns' and semantic memory 'distills them into a semantic memory to avoid information loss' (p. 2, p. 4) — raw interactions are condensed into compact narrative/fact form, not merely appended or freely synthesised into unrelated new insights.

The subconscious store is built 'to support efficient semantic retrieval' and stored units enable 'efficient similarity-based retrieval in future turns' (p. 4, p. 13); the consolidation step itself retrieves 'the set N_i containing the top-k units ranked by cosine similarity' (p. 4). No structured query, recency window, or declared multi-signal fusion rule for RecMem's own retrieval is described in the extracted pages.

RecMem is 'empirically evaluate[d] ... on two challenging long-term memory benchmarks (i.e., LoCoMo ... and LongMemEval-S)' against three baseline systems, reporting accuracy and token-cost comparisons (p. 2). No deployment, real users, or fielded setting is reported in the extracted pages, so this is lab-based benchmark validation, coded conservatively as validation rather than evaluation.
Results are reported as accuracy and memory-construction token cost on named benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S) against three SOTA baselines (MemoryOS, A-Mem, Mem0), per Figure 1(c)-(d) (p. 2).

The contributions list (p. 2) centres on 'recurrence-based consolidation' as a technique for deciding when to run LLM-based memory extraction; code is released (p. 1, GitHub link) but the paper argues for the consolidation technique itself, not the artefact.

title: E-mem: Multi-agent based Episodic Context Reconstruction for LLM Agent Memory
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 6, 14, 17, 21, 22, 23 of 23; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: Assistant agents each maintain an uncompressed episodic memory context built from prior conversation ('Memory Building, where long memory is processed into persistent episodic contexts', Appendix H, p. 14); at query time a routing mechanism selects and re-activates these stored segments so the master agent can condition its answer on them, tested across multi-session dialogue turns in the LoCoMo benchmark (p. 1, p. 2, p. 6). This is a run-time-written, cross-turn-retrieved agent memory store, not a fixed corpus or parametric-only mechanism, so no exclusion criterion applies.

facets.justification: Assistant agents 'maintain uncompressed memory contexts' rather than converting them into embeddings or graphs (p. 1-2); Appendix G states dormant agents are 'stored entirely on inexpensive disk storage (occupying only about 30KB per agent, which includes raw text, summaries, and embeddings)' (p. 14) — the primary content is raw text held per agent, with embeddings used only as a routing signal (see secondary_substrates).

The paper's stated motivation is avoiding 'destructive de-contextualization' from compression (p. 1); Appendix H describes 'Memory Building, where long memory is processed into persistent episodic contexts' (p. 14) with no rewriting or synthesis of existing entries described in the given pages — segments are preserved raw and appended, not compacted or rewritten.

Appendix I describes a 'Two-Stage Cascaded Routing Algorithm': a threshold override immediately activates a chunk if any of Svec, Skw or Sglobal exceeds a threshold, otherwise remaining chunks are ranked by a declared weighted sum w1*S~global + w2*S~vec + w3*S~kw to fill the activation budget (p. 14) — an explicit, declared fusion rule over vector, keyword and global-alignment signals.

Evaluated on the public LoCoMo and HotpotQA benchmarks against baselines (Long-Context, RAG, A-mem, Mem0, MemoryOS, LightMem, GAM) with F1/BLEU-1 tables (Table 1, Table 2, p. 6) and further ablations (document-shuffling robustness, storage overhead, retriever choice, Appendix F-I, p. 14); no deployed system or real users are reported in the given pages, so this is lab-controlled validation, coded conservatively.

Table 1 reports F1/BLEU-1 on the LoCoMo benchmark across five sub-tasks and two backbones against seven baselines; Table 2 reports F1 on HotpotQA at three context scales (p. 6) — a fixed task suite with scores, not a manipulated controlled condition or a deployment case study.

The contribution list on p. 2 names 'Heterogeneous Hierarchical Master-Assistant Architecture. We propose E-mem, a scalable framework that decouples high-level planning from memory retention,' i.e. the paper argues for a system architecture (master agent plus SLM-based assistant agents) rather than a single portable technique; code is released (p. 1) but the architecture itself is what is argued for.

title: Speculate with Memory: Lossless Acceleration for LLM Agents
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 4, 9, 17, 19, 20, 21 of 21; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: Section 2.2 (p. 4) equips the speculator with three online memory systems — a contrastive transition table, an episodic memory, and a confusion tracker — that accumulate from past agent trajectories at run time and are queried on later episodes/tasks to condition the speculator's own future predictions. The abstract and p. 1 state that gains 'grow continuously as memory accumulates' as more episodes are completed, i.e. state written in one episode conditions behaviour in later ones, satisfying I1. Published 2026 (I2), English (I3), and full text was retrievable (I4). None of E1–E7 apply: the memory captures action-sequence statistics, retrieved trajectory segments, and recurring-error patterns with explicit cross-episode semantics rather than being a stateless inference/cache optimisation (not E1, p. 1: 'existing speculators are stateless and discard all information between tasks'); an externalised store exists beyond the parametric speculator model (not E2); the stores are written online by the system itself, not fixed (not E3, p. 4); this is primary research with benchmark results, not a review (not E4); memory is the paper's central, title-level contribution (not E5); the system is an LLM-based agent pipeline (actor + LLM speculator) (not E6); and the paper is a full 21-page submission (not E7).

facets.justification: Section 2.2 (p. 4): the episodic memory embeds the current context with OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small (1536 dim) and retrieves the top-k most similar past episodes via cosine similarity — an embedding store the speculator itself writes online from trajectories. This is the component present in every benchmark's best-performing configuration in Table 7 (p. 19: Epi+Miss, Episodic, or the full Memory setting). The other two stores (contrastive transition table, confusion tracker) serve different purposes — aggregate action statistics and error suppression — and are not fused with episodic retrieval via any declared ranking rule (p. 4), so per the guide's 'different purposes, not multi_store' boundary they are recorded as secondary rather than coded as a combined substrate.

p. 4: completed episodes are stored as new trajectory segments (context, actions, observation, arg_sources, outcome, lesson); the 'lesson' field is 'auto-generated from episode metadata via template rules' and 'all episode fields are constructed by rule-based heuristics without auxiliary LLM calls' — which rules out reflect_synthesize, since no model-generated higher-level content is produced. No text on pp. 1, 2, 4, 9, 17, 19–20 describes existing episodic entries being rewritten, merged or deleted, ruling out edit_in_place.
p. 4: 'the current context is embedded ... and the top-k most similar episodes are retrieved via cosine similarity, providing the speculator with structured examples of similar past situations.'

Evaluated by replay against six public benchmarks (WebArena, ALFWorld, VWA, PDDL, τ²-bench, HotpotQA) against a Stateless baseline with significance testing (Table 7, p. 19). Appendix B.4 (p. 19) states directly: 'Our replay-based design evaluates speculation accuracy in isolation ... A live deployment study incorporating real API latencies is necessary to measure true end-to-end wall-clock savings and validate that the accuracy measured during replay translates to a proportional speedup in practice' — confirming no deployed, real-stakes setting was studied, only controlled benchmark comparison. Coded conservatively per the guide's validation/evaluation boundary.

Section 4 (p. 9) and Table 7 (p. 19): seven progressive memory settings are run across six fixed benchmark suites, reporting accuracy and latency-reduction scores against a Stateless baseline, with McNemar's-test significance per benchmark.

Contributions list, p. 2: 'We augment speculative execution for LLM agents with three complementary memory systems that accumulate experience from past trajectories: a contrastive transition table, an episodic memory with miss-episode recording, and a confusion tracker.' This is framed as a technique/algorithm augmenting an existing pipeline; none of the given pages describe a released tool or artefact as the thing being argued for.

title: From Storage to Steering: Memory Control Flow Attacks on LLM Agents
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 3, 7, 13, 26, 27, 28 of 28; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: The paper's own contribution list (p. 2) names four things: (1) identifying Memory Control Flow Attacks (MCFA) as a security threat, (2) a taxonomy of control-flow deviation types, (3) the MEMFLOW automated evaluation/attack framework, and (4) a large-scale evaluation of MCFA against GPT-5 mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash. Memory is central to the threat model but is not part of the claimed contribution itself, which is the attack/evaluation methodology, so this falls under E5.

title: From Memory to Skills: Evidence-Grounded Co-Evolution Governance for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 6, 17, 18, 25, 26, 27 of 27; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: MSCE writes L1 trace memory, L2 policy memory, and L3 environmental cognition at run time after each episode (Algorithm 2, 'Upon episode finalization: ... Write traces with V = pending', p. 18) and retrieves that same governed memory hierarchy in later episodes to condition future behaviour ('At inference time, MSCE retrieves memory in three tiers', p. 18); the agent itself authors the store rather than reading a fixed corpus (Section 4.4, p. 6). Published 2026, English, full text available (27 pages) — I2, I3, I4 hold. No exclusion criterion applies: memory writing/retrieval is the paper's central contribution (not E5), an externalised store is written at run time (not E2 or E3), it is an LLM-based agent system (not E6), and it is well over four pages with a full experiments section (not E7).

facets.justification: The contribution list names a three-level hierarchy — 'L1 trace memory stores grounded step-level evidence. L2 policy memory induces recurring procedural patterns... L3 environmental cognition memory abstracts declarative knowledge' (p. 2) — plus a crystallized skill store, and Appendix B.9 states the retrieval mechanism explicitly as tiering: 'At inference time, MSCE retrieves memory in three tiers' with skills tried first, L3 providing priors, and fallback to L1 traces (p. 6, p. 18). The combination/routing across these tiers is itself the paper's framework contribution, not an incidental detail.

L3 environmental cognition is produced by an LLM call over a cohort of policies and traces that is not any single source item ('d ← LLM(Πenv , C, T )', Algorithm 1, p. 17), and skills are crystallized by an LLM from an L2 policy plus evidence into a new callable procedure (Appendix E.5 skill-drafting prompt, p. 25). Step values are also produced via 'reflection-weighted value backfilling', propagating self-reflections ρ into computed trace values V (Eq. 2, p. 6) — generated content not present in the raw trace.

Appendix B.9 (p. 18) states a declared multi-signal combination for both tiers used at inference: skill retrieval is 'ranked by trigger relevance, reliability η, and source-policy gain', and trace retrieval 'combines exact cues such as error signatures with semantic similarity over compact state summaries', with high-value traces prioritized — an explicit fusion of exact/structured matching, similarity search, and a value-based ranking rule.

Evidence is 'Experiments on EvoAgentBench and LoCoMo' comparing MSCE against 'state-of-the-art skill-augmented and memory-driven agent baselines' (Abstract, p. 1; contributions list, p. 2). This is a controlled lab comparison on public benchmarks, not a fielded system with real users or deployment consequences, so it is coded validation rather than evaluation.

The stated evidence is comprehensive evaluation over two fixed benchmark suites, EvoAgentBench and LoCoMo, against multiple baselines with reported performance gains (contributions list, p. 2: 'Comprehensive evaluations on EvoAgentBench and LoCoMo show that MSCE achieves state-of-the-art performance'). No manipulated experimental condition against a held control beyond the benchmark/baseline comparison is described in the pages given.

The first item of the contributions list on p. 2 names the contribution as a framework: 'We propose MSCE, a training-free memory–skill co-evolution framework that organizes long-horizon agent experience into grounded traces, procedural policies, and declarative environmental cognition.' Code is released (p. 1, GitHub link), but the paper argues for the architecture/organisation itself rather than the artefact.

title: Trust, Lies, and Long Memories: Emergent Social Dynamics and Reputation in Multi-Round Avalon with LLM Agents

eligibility_reason: Agents play repeated Avalon games and, after each game, write a self-generated reflection (self-assessment plus per-player observations) that persists into subsequent games as memory and is referenced in later strategic reasoning — e.g. role-conditional reputation statements and the quoted 'I'm wary of repeating last game's mistake...' (p. 1 abstract/Figure 1 caption; contributions list, p. 2). The write prompt itself is given in Appendix A.8, 'Post-Game Reflection Prompt' (p. 8). This is an externalised, agent-written, cross-session store conditioning future behaviour, satisfying I1. Year 2026 satisfies I2, the paper is in English (I3), and full text pages were retrievable (I4). facets.justification: Retrieval candidates are ranked primarily by dense similarity from a FAISS IndexFlatIP index over BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 embeddings of the stored memory entries, with BM25 as a secondary lexical channel (Table 7, p. 14; “Dense relevance is the inner product of the normalized query and memory vectors,” p. 13). M<(t+1) = M<t ∪ {xt}” (p. 4), and “Entries are indexed only after episode finalization” (p. 13).

Full MERIT combines dense and BM25 scores with a stated fusion rule, r(x,u) = 0.75·dense + 0.25·BM25, after independent min-max normalization within each polarity pool (p. 13; also p. 14 Table 7, ‘Main ranking 0.75·s_dense + 0.25·s_BM25’). The contribution list on p. 2 centers on formulating causal episodic memory for repair and proposing the error-guided hybrid retrieval technique (“We propose error-guided hybrid retrieval that organizes repair experience by outcome and failure type...”); the controlled evaluation is listed as the third, supporting contribution, not an artefact being argued for.

p.5: the memory written at step t-1 directly becomes the inference context at step t (πθ(st | q, smem t-1)) — there is no similarity search, query, or agent-issued lookup described; the compressed memory is simply always the context for the next step, pairing with the prompt_resident substrate.

p.6, Table 1: MemPO is compared against ReAct, DeepResearcher, ReSearch, A-MEM, MEM1 and a no-memory GRPO baseline on synthesized multi-objective HotpotQA/NQ task sets under local-wiki and web-search conditions, with an ablation on the memory reward (p.6, 'Ablation study' paragraph). This is a controlled lab comparison on constructed benchmarks; no deployment, real users, or fielded system is reported in the pages given.

p.6, Table 1 reports F1, EM, total tokens (TT) and peak tokens (PT) for MemPO against six baselines across 2/4/6/8/10-objective task suites under two search-engine conditions — a fixed task suite with scores, which is the paper's central evidence (p.5–6, Sections 5.1–5.4).

p.2 contributions list: "We propose MemPO, a self-memory policy optimization algorithm, which effectively addresses credit assignment and steers the <mem> action toward retaining the most relevant information." title: AndroTMem: From Interaction Trajectories to Anchored Memory in Long-Horizon GUI Agents
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 9, 11, 24, 30, 31, 32 of 32; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: ASM (Anchored State Memory) has the GUI agent maintain a memory bank of state anchors that it writes at run time during task execution and reads back at every subsequent step to condition its next action: 'the agent maintains a memory bank of anchors and interacts with ASM in a retrieve–reason–update manner... At each step, the agent retrieves anchors conditioned on the current UI state and user instruction... After that, the agent analyzes the current step to determine whether new anchors should be created, whether existing anchors should be updated or invalidated' (p. 11). The system is an MLLM-driven GUI agent acting over Android apps (p. 1). No exclusion applies: it is not a hardware/cache optimisation, the store is externalised and agent-written (not parametric-only), the agent writes to the store rather than reading a fixed corpus, this is a primary study (a benchmark plus a proposed mechanism, not a survey), memory is the paper's central contribution, and the paper is 32 pages with full text available.

facets.justification: The memory bank stores discrete state anchors connected by explicit causal links that the agent writes and later traverses: 'ASM explicitly models the causal dependencies between anchors. Each anchor may optionally include a causal link that connects it to a previously generated anchor, forming a lightweight dependency structure... By organizing anchors together with their causal links, ASM forms a structured interaction memory rather than a flat list of events' (p. 24); Figure 1 depicts the anchor bank as linked nodes joined by 'Causal Link' edges (p. 2).

At each step the agent both creates new anchors/links and revises the existing bank: 'the agent analyzes the current step to determine whether new anchors should be created, whether existing anchors should be updated or invalidated, and whether new dependency links should be added to the memory bank' (p. 11). The paper frames this updateable revision, not mere appending, as ASM's defining advantage over raw replay and summaries: it 'preserves dependency-critical intermediate states in a grounded, structured, and updateable form' (p. 11).

Retrieval is filtered by the causal-dependency structure rather than a similarity ranking: 'the agent can retrieve anchors that are causally relevant to the current subgoal or context' and 'this allows the agent to retrieve only causally relevant anchors instead of processing the entire interaction history' (p. 24), formalized as Â_t = Retrieve(s_t, A_{t-1}) over the anchor bank (p. 11).

The evaluation runs 12 GUI agents (5 open-source, 5 closed-source, 2 multi-agent, per Fig. 1, p. 2) on the authors' own AndroTMem-Bench, reporting TCR/AMS against Raw History and Summary baselines (Table 3, p. 9; Figures 4-5, p. 11). This is a controlled lab comparison on an authors'-own benchmark, with no deployment or real users reported in the given pages, so it is coded validation rather than evaluation.

Table 3 (p. 9) reports per-intent AMS and TCR for 12 agents across seven task categories on the fixed AndroTMem-Bench suite (1,069 tasks, avg. 32.1 steps/task, p. 1), and Figures 4-5 (p. 11) compare Raw History, Summary, and ASM over that same benchmark's step ranges and task categories.

The abstract's headline proposal is the ASM mechanism itself — 'we propose Anchored State Memory (ASM), which represents interaction sequences as a compact set of causally linked intermediate-state anchors' (p. 1) — evaluated for the performance gains the paper reports (TCR +5%-30.16%, p. 1). The paper also releases the AndroTMem-Bench dataset and code (p. 1), but the technique is what the paper argues for, so the dataset is treated as a secondary artifact rather than the primary contribution.

title: Beyond Semantic Organization: Memory as Execution State Management for Long-Horizon Agents
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 15, 16, 17 of 17; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: MAGE stores the agent's own action-observation trace and derived subgoal summaries in a persistent tree at run time (Grow, Compress; Section 3, p. 4) and later reconstructs its execution state by reading the active root-to-current path on subsequent steps to condition future actions (p. 2, p. 4). This is an LLM-based agent (ReAct with a Qwen backbone, p. 7) that writes and reads its own externalised store across steps, published 2026, in English, with retrievable full text — satisfies I1-I4. Not E2/E3: the store is agent-written, not a fixed corpus (contrasted explicitly with static RAG corpora, p. 3). Not E4/E5/E6/E7: a novel 17-page method paper with memory as the stated contribution, evaluated empirically (p. 7).

facets.justification: MAGE writes a two-layer hierarchical execution-state tree: a bottom layer of raw action-observation nodes and a top layer of subgoal summary nodes, built by explicit parent/child node operations (Section 3.1-3.2, p. 4; Algorithm 1, p. 7). The paper explicitly distinguishes this from graph-based agent memory that organizes entries 'through entity or event relations' (Section 2.2, p. 3) and from vector stores retrieved by embedding similarity (p. 1, p. 3) — it is a state-management tree, not a semantic/knowledge graph, so none of the listed store types fit cleanly.

Compress 'moves completed raw segments from R into top-layer summaries in C, freeing context while preserving subgoal boundaries' (Section 3.2, p. 4), which is the mechanism the paper credits with bounding context growth (Abstract, p. 1; p. 4). Grow (append) and Revise (delete/restore to a boundary, an edit-in-place operation, Algorithm 1 R EVISE, p. 7) also transform the store, but the paper's headline claim and token-reduction result (55.1%, p. 1, p. 7) are attributed to the grow+compress boundary-aware compression cycle.

The execution state is read by traversing the tree from root to the current node — an exact structural traversal, not a ranking: 'the current execution state is read from the active tree path instead of being assembled from semantically similar entries' (Section 1, p. 2); Algorithm 1's TRACE and FLATTEN operations walk cover_nodes/parent pointers along this path (p. 7).

MAGE is evaluated on the MemoryArena benchmark against six baseline systems (HippoRAG2, MemoRAG, Mem0, ReasoningBank, MemoryOS, SimpleMem) with a fixed backbone LLM and controlled hyperparameters, reporting success rate, progress score and token consumption (Section 4, p. 7). No deployment, real users, or fielded setting is reported in the given pages — this is a lab benchmark comparison.

Section 4 (p. 7) runs a fixed task suite (MemoryArena, four domains) across MAGE and multiple baselines under identical model/hardware settings and reports scored metrics (SR, PS, token count) in a results table, matching benchmark evaluation rather than a single manipulated-condition experiment.

The contribution list (Section 1, p. 2) names the technique itself: 'We propose MAGE, which organizes agentic memory as a two-layer hierarchical tree... We design four coupled operations that make this tree an agent-manipulable object.' The contribution argued for is the mechanism, not a released tool or a dataset (MemoryArena is cited as an existing benchmark, not this paper's contribution).

title: AdMem: Advanced Memory for Task-solving Agents
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 14, 15, 16 of 16; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: Section 2.2 defines an actor agent that maintains a short-term memory state per turn, cleared at task end and encoded into a long-term memory store M managed by a separate memory agent; the critic agent generates procedural memory entries from observed outcomes, and these are later retrieved by the actor to condition future decisions (p. 4). Section 2.5 describes run-time writes (generation, merging, pruning) and retrieval of that store (pp. 6-7). This is an externalised store the agent itself writes and later reads across turns, meeting I1. Year 2026 (arXiv 2606.06787, p. 1) satisfies I2; text is English (I3); pages were retrievable (I4). No exclusion applies: the store is written by the agent at run time, not fixed (rules out E3) or exclusively parametric (rules out E2); it is not a hardware/cache paper (E1); not a survey (E4); memory is the entire claimed contribution, not incidental (E5); the system is an LLM-based multi-agent architecture (rules out E6); the paper runs to at least 16 pages with a full method and experiments section (rules out E7).

facets.justification: Abstract states the contribution is 'a unified and automatic memory framework that integrates semantic, episodic, and procedural memory in a bi-level design combining short-term and long-term stores' (p. 1). Figure 1 and Section 2.2 show a prompt-resident short-term store (stack-based context compaction, Section 2.4, p. 6) deliberately combined with a long-term store holding a 'Semantic Heap' and 'Episodic Stack' retrieved via dense embedding search (p. 4, p. 6). The bi-level combination itself, not either tier alone, is what the paper argues for.

Section 2.3's critic-agent tool ('generate procedural memory') requires a 'reflection' field: 'Think about what can be learned from the result of the action... what should the agent do under the same circumstances' (p. 14) — content not present in any single trajectory step, generated by comparing expected vs. actual outcome (p. 4). This is the mechanism the evaluation centers on (procedural-memory ablation vs. AWM/ReAct baselines, p. 7). Merge/prune of existing entries (edit_in_place) also occurs during long-term management (p. 6) but is a secondary, not the evaluated, transformation.

Section 2.5-3 gives a declared fusion rule for procedural memory: score = v_m * psi(c_t)^T * psi(c_m), combining a learned effectiveness/utility estimate v_m with dense context-similarity, and memories are retrieved greedily by top-n of that combined score (p. 6-7). Semantic and episodic memory use plain dense (similarity) retrieval (p. 6), so the paper explicitly combines a similarity signal with a separate learned-value re-ranking rule for its central retrieval mechanism.

Section 3 (p. 7) states the system is 'tested on a variety of task domains bundled by the implementation of AgentBoard environment' against baselines ReAct and AWM, reporting task completion and average progress. Despite language describing conditions that 'simulate real task-solving agent environments', this is a public benchmark comparison with no real users or deployed setting reported in the given pages — the conservative, benchmark-scored reading is validation.

Section 3 (p. 7): fixed task suite (AgentBoard, spanning embodied AI, text games, web research, tool calling), fixed system prompts, baselines (ReAct, AWM), and reported metrics (task completeness percentage, average progress p_i) in Table 1.

Abstract (p. 1) and Section 2.2 heading 'Framework' with Figure 1 (p. 4) describe the contribution as an architecture: a multi-agent system (actor, memory, critic agents) organizing a bi-level, multi-type (semantic/episodic/procedural) memory store — an organizing system rather than a single technique, tool release, or dataset.

title: Imprint: Online Memory Compression for Long-Horizon Egocentric QA
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 4, 5, 15, 16, 17, 18 of 18; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: Imprint is an LLM-driven pipeline (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct throughout, per p. 5) that writes structured Interaction Records into an evolving memory M at run time as new observations arrive, via a three-stage online compression process — Event-Prototype Assignment, Interaction Importance filtering, and Interaction Consolidation (p. 2, p. 4 Fig. 2 caption) — and later retrieves top-k entries from that same self-written memory to condition each new question's answer (p. 4, Section 3.3, Eq. 3). This is a run-time write followed by cross-query retrieval over a store the system itself populates, not retrieval over a fixed corpus (E3 does not apply). No hardware/cache optimisation (E1), no parametric-only memory (E2), no secondary study (E4), memory is the entire contribution not incidental (E5), and the paper is well over four pages with full evaluation (E7 does not apply).

facets.justification: Memory entries are compared and merged via cosine similarity of contextual and action-object embeddings (event-prototype threshold δg = 0.75, consolidation threshold δm = 0.75, p. 4–p. 5), and retrieval ranks candidate entries with a weighted cosine-similarity score over object/action embeddings, Eq. 3 (p. 4). No separate structured schema, graph, or file store is described in the given pages.

The paper frames its write mechanism explicitly as 'online memory compression': incoming records are filtered by an importance score and then 'merged with similar observations into the compact memory M (Interaction Consolidation)' (p. 4, Fig. 2 caption); p. 2 describes the same process as producing 'compact long-term memories' as records arrive, reducing memory footprint 2.3× (p. 1).

Base retrieval ranks memory entries by a declared weighted-cosine top-k score, Eq. 3 (p. 4: sk = γ1 cos(eoq,eok) + γ2 cos(eaq,eak) + γ3 w(fk), TopK selected). For questions with temporal constraints, this ranked set is then explicitly filtered by a declared rule using first_time/last_time/before/after predicates to produce the final evidence set R' (p. 4, Section 3.3) — a stated fusion of similarity ranking and structured filtering.

Evaluation is confined to the public EgoLifeQA benchmark (500-question subset for participant Jake) against a reproduced EgoRAG baseline under a controlled LLM setup, run on a single NVIDIA L40 GPU (p. 5). No deployed system, real users, or field setting appears in the given pages.

EgoRAG is deliberately reproduced with the same LLM (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) and captioner 'to isolate the contribution of memory representation from LLM capacity... ensuring that performance differences arise from memory representation and retrieval design' (p. 5) — a manipulated-condition-vs-control design, further corroborated by systematic component-removal ablations (Table 5, stage-wise removal of Event-Prototype Assignment / Interaction Importance / Interaction Consolidation, and Table 8, zeroing each Eq. 3 term, both p. 15).

Self-described throughout as an architecture rather than a single technique: abstract calls it 'an interaction-centric memory framework' (p. 1), and the contributions list on p. 2 introduces 'Imprint, a cognitively inspired online memory compression framework' spanning pattern discovery, importance estimation, and consolidation stages.

title: LLMs in the Imaginarium: Tool Learning through Simulated Trial and Error
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 4, 10, 16, 21, 22, 23 of 23; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: The paper's contribution (Simulated Trial and Error, STE) has the LLM write a long-term memory of past-explored queries and whether they were fulfilled during the exploration stage, and that store is reloaded into context at the start of every subsequent trial to condition what the model imagines next (p. 4: 'the long-term memory records the past-explored queries and whether they were judged as successfully fulfilled ... It is only loaded into the context at the beginning of every new trial'). A short-term memory of recent trial trajectories serves the same run-time write/read role within an episode (p. 2, Figure 1 caption). Published 2024 at ACL (p. 1), in English, and full text was retrievable (22 pages, well over the E7 four-page floor). Memory is not incidental: the abstract names it as one of three orchestrated mechanisms and both memories are separately ablated (Tables 15-16, pp. 21-22).

facets.justification: The long-term memory (past-explored queries + fulfilled status) is not queried by similarity or structure; it is loaded wholesale into the prompt at the start of each new trial, so nothing is queried out of it at retrieval time (p. 4: 'It is only loaded into the context at the beginning of every new trial'). Figure 1c (p. 2) depicts it as a table of 'Explored Queries / Fulfilled?' fed directly into the next trial's context.

P. 4: the long-term memory 'records the past-explored queries and whether they were judged as successfully fulfilled' and 'serves as a growing pool of past successes and failures' as exploration proceeds — new entries accumulate; the text on the given pages does not describe any rewriting, merging, or deletion of prior entries.

P. 4: the long-term memory 'is only loaded into the context at the beginning of every new trial' with no stated selection, ranking, or query step over its contents — the whole store re-enters context each trial.

STE is a novel technique tested via comprehensive experiments on APIs drawn from ToolBench against baselines (ToolLLaMA-v2, GPT-4, Mistral-Instruct-7B) (p. 1 abstract, p. 4 Baselines & exploitation with STE). No deployment, real users, or fielded system is reported on any given page.

P. 1: 'Comprehensive experiments on Tool-Bench show that STE substantially improves tool learning for LLMs ... bringing a boost of 46.7% to Mistral-Instruct-7B and enabling it to outperform GPT-4' — a fixed API/task suite with correctness-rate scores compared across multiple baseline models (p. 2 bullet findings: GPT-4 60.8%, ToolLLaMA-v2 37.3%).

The paper's own framing centers on STE as a technique ('a biologically inspired method for tool-augmented LLMs, simulated trial and error (STE)', p. 1 abstract); code/data are released (p. 1 footnote) but the argued contribution is the mechanism, not the artefact itself.

title: ES-MemEval: Benchmarking Conversational Agents on Personalized Long-Term Emotional Support
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13 of 13; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: The contribution is a benchmark (ES-MemEval) and an accompanying static multi-session dataset (EvoEmo) for evaluating memory capabilities of existing LLM systems on QA, summarization and dialogue-generation tasks over a fixed pre-recorded conversation transcript (p. 1, abstract: 'we introduce ES-MemEval, a comprehensive benchmark...To support the benchmark, we also propose EvoEmo, a multi-session dataset'). The evaluated systems are off-the-shelf long-context models fed the full given history, and RAG variants where 'a dense retriever (bge-m3) retrieves the top-4 most relevant full-session contexts from a FAISS index to supply user information' (p. 6, Section 5). In both cases the store being read is the fixed, pre-existing dialogue transcript supplied as benchmark input, not a store the agent itself writes to at run time during the interaction; no page given describes an agent deciding what to write into a memory store or a write-then-later-retrieve loop that conditions the agent's own future behaviour (I1 not met). This matches E3: retrieval over a fixed corpus the agent never writes to.

title: On Memory Construction and Retrieval for Personalized Conversational Agents
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 34, 35, 36 of 36; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: The system constructs a memory bank M from the running conversation history H, where each memory unit corresponds to a turn, session, or (in the proposed method) a topically coherent segment of turns already exchanged, including the agent's own prior responses (p. 4, Section 2.1: 'each turn t_j = (u_j, r_j) consisting of a user request u_j and the corresponding response from the agent r_j'; 'Memory construction: construct a memory bank M using conversation history H'). This history accrues at run time as the dialogue proceeds and is later retrieved ('Memory retrieval: given a target user request u* and context budget N, retrieve N memory units... relevant to user request u*', p. 4) to condition the agent's next response ('Response generation: take the retrieved N memory units... as the context and query the response generation model', p. 4). This is a run-time write-then-retrieve loop conditioning future behaviour, not retrieval over a fixed corpus the agent never writes to (E3 does not apply). Published as an ICLR 2025 paper (p. 1), in English, full-length with extensive experiments (p. 1-4, 10, 34-36), so I2-I4 and E7 are satisfied/not triggered. No exclusion criterion applies.

facets.justification: Memory units (turn/session/segment) are retrieved by a base retrieval system f_R; results are reported separately for a 'BM25 based retriever' and an 'MPNet based retriever' (p. 3, Figure 2b/2c, Figure 3), with MPNet an embedding model used for similarity-based retrieval over the constructed memory units. No graph, relational, filesystem, or KV-cache structure is described in the given pages, and there is no declared multi-store combination, so vector_store (embedding similarity search over agent-written conversation units) is the best-supported value.

Memory construction is defined as partitioning existing conversation history into memory units (turns, sessions, or segments) without rewriting prior content (p. 4, Section 2.1-2.2: segmentation model f_I splits session c into segments {s_k}). The paper explicitly states response generation 'directly concatenate[s] the retrieved segment-level memory units as the context... bypassing summarization to avoid the information loss that often occurs when converting dialogues into summaries' (p. 3), which rules out summarize_compress or reflect_synthesize for the stored memory content itself. The compression-based denoising (LLMLingua-2) described in the contributions (p. 4) is applied to enhance retrieval matching, not to replace or rewrite the stored memory units used as context; the mechanics of that step are in Section 2.3, which was not among the given pages, so this justification is limited to what pp. 3-4 establish about the stored content.

Retrieval is defined as selecting a fixed number of memory units under a context budget N (p. 4, Section 2.1), and the reported evaluations sweep 'K: number of retrieved segments' / 'Number of Retrieved Turns' against retrieval accuracy (DCG) for both a BM25 and an MPNet-based retriever (p. 3, Figure 2b/2c, Figure 3). This is top-k ranked retrieval by relevance score, not an exact structured query, a fixed recency window, or an agent-issued read, and no declared fusion rule combining the two retrievers is given, so hybrid does not apply.

The paper reports controlled comparisons against baselines on public long-term-conversation benchmarks: 'Experimental results show that SeCom exhibits a significant performance advantage over baselines on long-term conversation benchmarks LOCOMO and Long-MT-Bench+' (p. 1 abstract; repeated p. 4 contributions and p. 10 conclusion). No deployed system, real users, or fielded setting is reported in the given pages, so this is lab-based technique investigation, not evaluation-in-practice.

Results are reported as scores over fixed benchmark suites (LOCOMO, Long-MT-Bench+, and dialogue-segmentation datasets DialSeg711, TIAGE, SuperDialSeg per p. 1 abstract) with baseline comparisons and ablations ('Further analysis and ablation studies confirm the contributions of the segment-level memory units and the compression-based denoising technique', p. 10), matching benchmark_evaluation rather than a single controlled manipulation, case study, simulation, or proof-of-concept.

The contributions list (p. 3-4) centers on two techniques: a conversation segmentation method for constructing segment-level memory, and a compression-based denoising technique for retrieval, packaged as 'SeCom, a system that constructs memory bank at segment level... while applying compression based denoising on memory units' (p. 4). A project page is linked (p. 1 footnote) but the paper argues for the segmentation and denoising techniques themselves, not for the released artefact as the contribution, so method fits better than tool or framework.

title: HERO: Human-profile Enhanced Retrieval Optimization Framework for Long-term Agent Memory
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 13, 14, 15 of 15; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: HERO converts dialogue history into a heterogeneous memory graph (Episodic Traces, Episodic Units, Episodic Cues, Profile Insights/Cues) written incrementally at run time as new dialogues arrive, and later queried by the agent to condition its answers on prior turns/sessions: 'HERO supports incremental updates: new dialogues create local nodes and edges (linking to the latest predecessor and merging new cues), without full graph reconstruction' (p. 4), and retrieval proceeds via a three-phase cue-activation/graph-traversal process over that same graph (p. 4). Published 2026 (arXiv, p. 1), English, full 15-page paper (extraction note), no exclusion criterion applies: it is not a hardware/cache paper (not E1), the store is externalized and agent-written, not purely parametric (not E2), the agent writes into the graph rather than only reading a fixed corpus (not E3), it is a primary method paper, not a survey (not E4), memory is the entire contribution, not incidental (not E5), and the system is explicitly framed as agent memory for long-horizon interactions (not E6).

facets.justification: The contribution list (p. 2) states 'We design a heterogeneous memory graph that preserves complete dialogue episodes as final evidence.' Page 4 describes nodes (Episodic Traces, Episodic Units, Episodic Cues, Profile Insights) and edges built via 'structural inclusion, semantic indexing, and temporal chaining,' with Table 8 (p. 12) reporting per-user node/edge counts, confirming the memory is stored and traversed as a graph the agent writes to.

The paper's contribution is framed explicitly against prior compression/rewriting approaches: the abstract and p. 2 contributions state HERO 'preserves raw dialogue text as evidence for reasoning, thereby mitigating information loss' rather than rewriting or replacing memories, and p. 4 states the Episodic Layer supports 'variable-resolution retrieval from coarse traces to fine-grained facts without irreversible compression,' with incremental updates that 'create local nodes and edges... without full graph reconstruction.' Profile Insights are described as guidance signals derived from traces, but p. 2 is explicit that 'these profile nodes act as navigational bridges rather than replacement memories' — the primary evidence store (Episodic Traces) is appended, not rewritten.

Page 4 declares a three-phase, explicitly combined retrieval procedure: '(1) Initial Anchor Identification' via embedding cosine-similarity thresholding against cue nodes, '(2) Iterative Context Expansion' via cue-context-cue graph traversal, and '(3) Global Relevance Propagation and Evidence Ranking' using 'Personalized PageRank initialization' (also described in the Figure 1 caption on p. 4) that combines activated Episodic-Unit and Profile-Insight cues. This is a stated fusion of similarity matching, graph traversal, and rank propagation, not a single unranked mechanism.

Evidence is drawn entirely from lab-style comparison: Table 6 (p. 12) compares HERO against baselines (MemoryOS, Mem0, MemU, MemOS, Zep, EverMemOS) on LoCoMo, ablations against HERO variants appear in Figure 2 (p. 8), and hyperparameter sensitivity is reported in Table 5 (p. 8) and Table 7 (p. 12) on the LoCoMo and PERSONAMEM benchmarks. No real users, deployment, or fielded system is reported in any given page; the Conclusion (p. 8) frames the results as validating the framework on benchmark datasets, not in a live setting.

The paper reports scores against baselines on two fixed benchmark datasets — LoCoMo (56.06% F1, per p. 2 contributions) and PERSONAMEM (70.63% accuracy) — with per-backbone comparison tables (Table 6, p. 12) and top-k sensitivity tables (Table 7, p. 12); this is a benchmark-suite comparison rather than a manipulated controlled-experiment condition or a bare proof-of-concept run.

The paper repeatedly self-identifies HERO as a 'framework' organizing two integrated components — graph-based memory construction and profile-guided retrieval — rather than a single algorithm: the title and abstract name it 'Human-profile Enhanced Retrieval Optimization framework for long-term agent memory,' and the contributions on p. 2 list both a construction design ('a heterogeneous memory graph') and a separate retrieval-mechanism design as parts of one architecture, with no released artifact/tool described in the given pages that would make 'tool' the better fit.

title: Generation-Based and Emotion-Reflected Memory Update: Creating the KEEM Dataset for Better Long-Term Conversation
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 17, 18, 19 of 19; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: The paper's central contribution is a generation-based memory-update mechanism for long-term conversational systems: given existing memory M (previous sessions' summaries) and the current session's summary S, the system writes an updated memory M^U that merges, resolves conflicts and preserves essential information, then that memory is what the system draws on to 'inquire about recent conditions and reference past conversations accurately' in later sessions (p. 1; Section 3.2, p. 4; Figure 1 example, p. 2). That is a run-time write of state that conditions later behaviour across sessions, satisfying I1. Published 2026, English, full text available (I2-I4). No exclusion criterion applies: the store is written by the system itself, not a fixed corpus (rules out E3); memory is externalised, not parametric (rules out E2); memory is the paper's explicit, named contribution, not incidental (rules out E5); this is a primary study with an original dataset/method, not a survey (rules out E4); the paper concerns a long-term conversational agent, not hardware/cache optimisation (rules out E1, E6); it is 19 pages (rules out E7).

facets.justification: Section 3.2 (p. 4) describes memory M as 'previous sessions' summaries' that is compared as a whole against the current session's summary S to produce an updated memory M^U; the few-shot examples (pp. 17-18) show the entire memory as a flat list of natural-language sentences fed directly into the prompt and rewritten as a whole. No vector index, graph, relational schema, filesystem, or KV-cache mechanism is described anywhere in the given pages -- the memory is a maintained, directly-reinserted text block, matching prompt_resident.

facets.justification: The paper's own title and Contribution 1 name the deliberate relationship between two stores as the contribution itself: 'the append-only event log is the source of truth; the working graph is a deterministic projection of that log' (p. 1-2). No exclusion criterion applies: the store is agent-written, not fixed (not E3); memory is externalised, not purely parametric (not E2); it is a primary system contribution, not incidental or a secondary study (not E4/E5); it is an LLM agent built on GPT5.2 / the OpenAI Agents SDK (p. 14), not E6; the paper is 17 pages with substantive content, not E7/E1.

facets.justification: Table 1 (p. 6) maps the user-profile state component u to 'USER.md + MEMORY.md' and the skill-repository state component S_skills to 'configs/skills/{name}/'. Writes are performed as file/document writes: ws.write_prompt("USER", u_profile), ws.write_prompt("MEMORY", memory), and ws.skill_set(sk.name, skill_to_md(sk)) (p. 15). Skills themselves are defined as multi-file structured packages with instructions and reference files (p. 2).

At session end, new_skills ← LLM_extract_skills(h) and Δmemory ← LLM_extract_memory_changes(h) generate skill/memory content by analyzing accumulated dialogue history rather than copying a single source item (Phase 4, p. 15). This matches the paper's own framing of 'extracting potential new skills or structurally optimizing existing skills based on accumulated usage data' (p. 5) — higher-level abstractions synthesized from session experience.

A single declared matching function M(u, S_skills) → skill ∪ {∅} (Eq. 1, p. 6) cascades through three stages with a stated combination rule: exact keyword matching, then (only if that fails) embedding cosine-similarity matching against a threshold, then (only if that fails) LLM-based semantic classification (Eqs. 2-4, p. 6; Algorithm lines 8-44, p. 14). The matched skill is what gets injected into context, so retrieval for the coded substrate follows this declared three-way fallback pipeline.

The abstract (p. 1) reports results 'based on real-world foreign trade scenarios' scored by the authors under a 'five-dimensional LLM-as-Judge evaluation protocol,' with 'model transfer experiments' comparing underlying models. This reads as the authors' own structured test suite and judge-scored comparison rather than a fielded deployment with independent users or external stakes. The evaluation/discussion/conclusion pages (roughly pp. 7-13) were not included in the extracted pages, so this is coded conservatively as validation per the guide's default-to-validation instruction under ambiguity.

Abstract (p. 1) describes running the system over 'real-world foreign trade scenarios' and scoring outcomes with a fixed 'five-dimensional LLM-as-Judge evaluation protocol,' reporting an aggregate ~28% average-score improvement 'after integrating EvoAgent,' plus separate model-transfer runs across underlying models over the same protocol — the fixed-suite-plus-scoring pattern of benchmark_evaluation. The actual methodology/results section (Section 4) was not among the provided pages, so this is inferred from the abstract's description only.

The title names the contribution 'An Evolvable Agent Framework'; the four core innovations (p. 2) describe an architecture — a structured skill representation format, a skill self-evolution mechanism, and a hierarchical sub-agent delegation architecture — rather than a single algorithm, a released tool, or a dataset. Code/data release is mentioned in the abstract (p. 1) but is not itself what the paper argues for.

title: An Agent-Oriented Pluggable Experience-RAG Skill for Experience-Driven Retrieval Strategy Orchestration
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 of 7; front matter, tail, and the 2 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: The system's 'experience memory' stores records e = (scene features, score vector, best strategy, best margin) that the Strategy Router 'consults' to pick a retrieval strategy (p. 2, Section 2.2), and Section 2.3 describes it as 'reusable experience records' that are looked up (p. 3). No page describes the agent writing new entries to this store at run time: the strongest reported setting is a static 'rule-based routing' table mapping task types to fixed strategies ('maps direct tasks to dense, and both multi hop and scientific tasks to hybrid rrf', p. 2), and the learned-routing variants that were tried are reported as underperforming and not adopted (p. 2, and Appendix A.2 on p. 5). The evaluation in Section 3 (pp. 3) measures only retrieval quality (Recall@10/MRR@10/nDCG@10) against a fixed candidate pool, with no measurement of any write, update, or persistence-across-sessions process for the experience memory. This is retrieval over a store the agent is never shown writing to (E3); the pages given do not evidence the run-time write-and-later-retrieve-across-turns mechanism required by I1.

title: MemChain: Learning Interpretable Memory Traces for Memory-Augmented LLM Agents
extraction_note: pages 1, 2, 3, 9, 13, 17, 18, 19 of 19; front matter, tail, and the 3 middle page(s) densest in memory-mechanism vocabulary. Other pages were not extracted.
eligibility_reason: MemChain's own contribution is explicitly scoped to post-retrieval processing of an already-retrieved candidate set, not to writing the memory store. Section 2.1 states 'MemChain instead leaves M unchanged and learns the temporary mapping (q, Cq) -> E' (p. 3), and the introduction states 'MemChain leaves retrieval and memory writing fixed; it learns the post-retrieval transformation from Cq to E' (p. 2). The memory pool M is treated as a fixed store the mediator reads from but never writes to; its output E ('active memory') is 'exposed only to the frozen answer model' for the current query (p. 3), with no mechanism shown for E or any agent-authored content to persist into later turns or sessions. The Conclusion/Limitations even flag this as future work: 'Future work will... extend MemChain to richer, continually updated memory stores' (p. 9), confirming the present contribution does not update the store. This is retrieval/post-retrieval transformation over a fixed candidate pool (E3); it does not meet I1, since the claimed contribution contains no mechanism by which the agent itself writes state at run time for later cross-turn or cross-session retrieval.
